summary: AeroXpace is a web-based astronaut health and mission-control system built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. On deep-space missions, a message to Earth can take about 20 minutes one way, so a reply may arrive 40 minutes later. A sick or injured astronaut cannot wait that long. AeroXpace monitors 27 physiological and environmental parameters of an Axiom Mission 3 crew member in real time and warns of problems before limits are crossed. In an emergency it starts a step-by-step medical protocol immediately, sounding the alarm only on the device the astronaut is using (tablet, wristband or helmet HUD), while a live panel shows alerts still travelling to Earth. An offline AI assistant supports autonomous decisions. The system also uses real NASA DONKI space-weather data, models ISS orbit and radiation, and exports FHIR data. It works offline in English and Turkish. All crew telemetry is simulated and clearly labeled.
details:
The problem
On long missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts cannot rely on instant help from Earth. At deep-space distances a message can take about 20 minutes one way, so a question to Earth may not be answered for 40 minutes. A health emergency cannot wait that long. The astronaut needs a system that watches their health continuously, warns early, and guides them through emergencies on its own.

1. Live health monitoring
27 parameters in six groups: environment (CO₂, O₂, pressure, radiation, temperature), vital signs, neurological, muscle and bone, immune, and psychological. A health score summarizes everything, and each parameter shows normal, warning or critical status. A small hysteresis stops statuses from flickering at the limits.

2. Early warning
The system measures how fast each value is moving. If a value will cross its limit within about 90 seconds, it shows an estimated time to the limit before the alarm.

3. Emergency scenarios and device routing
Six scenarios (cardiac emergency, hypoxia, depressurization, radiation storm, heat stress, CO₂ build-up), each with four phases and a step-by-step protocol. Because Earth cannot answer in time, the protocol starts immediately without waiting for ground confirmation. The alarm sounds only on the device in use: tablet, wristband (with haptics) or helmet HUD. It is acknowledged by button or Enter on the tablet, the crown on the wristband, or a 2-second hold on the HUD.

4. Space environment
Real solar flare, CME, geomagnetic storm and particle events come from NASA CCMC DONKI (last 14 days) and raise the radiation level. The ISS is modeled on a circular orbit with the South Atlantic Anomaly (about 2.2× radiation), eight ground stations with signal-acquisition and loss times, and a running radiation dose with a forecast. If DONKI is unreachable, simulated data is used and labeled as such.

5. The 20-minute Earth ⇄ Space link
The Mission Control tab has a dedicated communication-delay display in a JARVIS-style ring design. The center shows the one-way delay as a large counter (for example 20:00) and the round trip below it (40:00). A live list shows each alarm, acknowledgement and telemetry frame as a packet travelling to Earth, with a countdown until Earth sees it and a “delivered” mark when it arrives. When the delay is long, the panel states that Earth’s reply arrives too late and the system is acting autonomously. The delay can be set to ISS relay (0.6 s), Moon (1.3 s), Mars closest (3 min), Mars average (12.5 min), deep space (20 min) or Mars farthest (22 min). A mission table also compares the astronaut’s live values with what Earth sees after the delay.

6. Mission profiles and autonomy
Four profiles: ISS, Moon (Artemis/Gateway), Mars transit and Deep space (20 min). Each changes the radiation baseline, alert thresholds and communication delay together. The built-in AI assistant answers from live data and works fully offline, so it keeps helping when Earth cannot answer in time.

7. Astronaut tools
CPR metronome (110 per minute, 30:2 cycles), SOS/Mayday, medical kit inventory, radiation shelter advisor, exercise mode (thresholds adapt to heart-rate zones), EVA go/no-go checklist, daily check-in, reminders, crew log, sleep tracker, crew comparison, breathing coach, and a bone and muscle countermeasure planner (illustrative model).

8. Data and interoperability
Export as FHIR R4 with LOINC codes, CSV report, JSON black box, or a printable PDF health report. Every alarm and event is logged.

9. Usability
English and Turkish, command palette (Ctrl+K), favorites bar, night mode, font size and high-contrast options, sound alerts, and every element opens a detail view. It is an installable web app that works offline.

10. Technology and honesty
Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks or build step, hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Crew telemetry, scenarios, ISS position and the communication delay are simulated. Only the space-weather feed is real NASA data. Medical content is educational, not medical advice, and the app says so.
